<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Contact variability remains a major obstacle for scaled two-dimensional transistors, yet whether electrode contact type can control the defect sensitivity of carrier-injection barriers remains unresolved. Here we show that double-sided recessed Ti contacts strongly stabilise MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    carrier-injection barriers against changes in sulfur-vacancy position. By comparing matched MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    model families based on one-sided top Ti contacts and double-sided recessed Ti contacts under the same ordered sulfur-vacancy sequence, first-principles electronic structure and non-equilibrium transport calculations reveal a clear contact-type dependence. For the near-edge vacancy, the Schottky barrier height (SBH) decreases from 0.58 eV for the one-sided top Ti contact to 0.21 eV for the double-sided recessed Ti contact, while the nominal position-dependent SBH variation is reduced by about 85%. Electron transmission calculations further show that this barrier stabilisation results in higher transmission and lower access energies for propagating channel states. The results identify double-sided recessed Ti contacts as a strategy for reducing sulfur-vacancy-induced barrier variability in Ti–MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    electronics.
                  </jats:p>
title: Defect-tolerant carrier injection in MoS2 enabled by double-sided recessed Ti contacts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Somatic mutations are postzygotic DNA alterations that accumulate throughout development and aging, underlying somatic mosaicism across cell populations. Neurons are particularly vulnerable due to oxidative stress, high metabolic demand, and age-related decline in DNA damage response pathways, promoting cell-type-specific dysfunction. Somatic repeat instability is an established driver in Huntington’s disease, yet the extent and functional impact of somatic mutagenesis in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis remains unresolved. This article highlights how advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing, integrated with computational and machine learning approaches, support detecting ultra-rare variants and establishing causal links between somatic mutagenesis and neurodegeneration.</jats:p>
title: Somatic mutations in neurodegeneration: from detection to disease mechanisms

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Molecular and reaction fingerprints are widely used as static descriptors, but their relationship to graph-level reaction application remains unclear. We address this question in counted Extended-Connectivity Fingerprint (ECFP) space, representing reactions as signed differences between product and substrate fingerprints. We define ECFP-compatible templates, for which graph-level reaction application induces a constant fingerprint displacement, yielding a functorial mapping from graph transformations to affine translations in fingerprint space. We also introduce reaction-center ECFPs to encode the local environments required for template application and to provide a fast coordinate-wise prefilter for graph-level reaction applicability. We evaluate this framework on USPTO-50k and MetaNetX reactions across a range of ECFP radii. Both representations carry predictive information for reaction-class and enzyme-class classification, with reaction-center ECFPs contributing information not captured by reaction ECFPs alone. This framework connects reaction templates and reaction fingerprints to molecular pathway search and reaction-property prediction in fingerprint space.</jats:p>
title: Representing chemical and enzymatic reactions in fingerprint space for applicability filtering and classification

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Identifying bioactive compounds for orphan or understudied protein targets remains a significant hurdle in drug discovery due to the lack of sufficient structure-activity relationship (SAR) data. We present MolFuSE (Molecular Function-guided Similarity Explorer), an unsupervised, projection-based enrichment framework designed for low-data virtual screening and ligand repurposing. MolFuSE leverages manifold learning—specifically uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)—to create low-dimensional similarity spaces based on a reference set of ligands known to bind proteins with the same molecular function as the target. Through systematic evaluation across nine protein targets and their functional classes, we demonstrate that UMAP embeddings of Mordred 2D descriptors act as a strong “potency filter”, significantly outperforming traditional topological fingerprints in the early enrichment of high-potency inhibitors (<100 nM). While extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP4) fingerprints achieve superior global ranking (receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-area under the curve (AUC) 0.961 vs. 0.863), the descriptor-based approach provides more robust early recognition (enrichment factor at 1% (EF@1%)) when the reference set itself is small. Crucially, we identify a critical point in data scaling: performance peaks at a reference set size of approximately 10,000 compounds and degrades for larger sets due to descriptor-space dilution from structurally diverse weak binders. MolFuSE provides a computationally efficient, interpretable tool for prioritizing high-affinity candidates when target-specific data is unavailable.  </jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Allodynia (pain in response to normally non-noxious stimuli) and hyperalgesia (increased sensitivity to painful stimuli) are well-established indicators of pain sensitization after tissue damage in vertebrates. These phenomena may also offer valuable insights into nociceptive processing in invertebrates. We assessed behavioural evidence for allodynia and hyperalgesia following two types of peripheral injury (tarsus amputation or burning) and sham treatment in black garden ants (
                      <jats:italic>Lasius niger</jats:italic>
                      , Hymenoptera: Formicidae). At 20 min, 24 h, and 96 h post-anaesthesia, a ramping hot plate assay with sublethal, but increasingly noxious, temperatures was used to assess allodynia and hyperalgesia. Locomotor speed and proportion of time spent moving were quantified to detect increased responsiveness at normally non-noxious temperatures (allodynia) or exaggerated responses at higher temperatures (hyperalgesia).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We observed an earlier onset of responsiveness in ants with tarsus amputations and burns compared to controls, consistent with allodynia, which was stronger and more consistent in tarsus-amputated ants and at later time points. Evidence for hyperalgesia was limited and time-dependent: amputated ants showed a steeper response increase at higher temperatures at earlier time points, but not at 96 h. Burn-treated ants showed less consistent evidence of allodynia and no evidence of hyperalgesia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that sensitization extends beyond the acute injury phase and align with broader evidence for chronic, pain-like processing in insects. As a new injury model in insects, the burn treatment needs to be refined, or the underlying mechanisms may be different to those involved in classic, amputation-induced sensitization.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Developing cost-effective and high-performance electrocatalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is essential for advancing anion-exchange membrane fuel cell technologies. In this study, we report a robust heterostructure formed by covalently functionalized carbon nanohorns (CNH-N) integrated with metallic 1T-MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    2D nanosheets. Through tailored diazonium chemistry, positively charged ammonium groups were introduced onto CNHs, enabling strong electrostatic and van der Waals interactions with negatively charged exfoliated MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    . Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirm successful functionalization, enhanced defect modulation, and intimate CNH–MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    coupling. The resulting CNH-N-MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    catalyst exhibits remarkable ORR performance, including an optimized onset potential of 0.80 V, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and a dominant four-electron reduction pathway with ~94% selectivity toward H
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O, which is comparable to commercial Pt/C. These results highlight how controlled chemical functionalization and heterointerface engineering can synergistically enhance catalytic activity and stabilize the 1T-MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    phase. The CNH-N-MoS
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    heterostructures thus represent a promising class of platinum-group-metal-free/low-metal-content electrocatalysts for efficient fuel cell applications.
                  </jats:p>
title: Enhanced electrocatalytic oxygen reduction to H₂O with high selectivity via 2D 1T-MoS₂ integrated with functionalized carbon nanohorns
